task.description: A skydiver carried by rocket to high altitude (possibly above the atmosphere) exits in a space suit with parachute and descends to Earth's surface. Total mass (skydiver + suit + parachute) = 190 kg. Analyze the challenges/dangers of such a descent and determine the maximum altitude from which a person could successfully descend to the surface.
task.target_quantity: max_altitude_km: maximum release altitude (km) such that the descent's peak |acceleration| stays within the safety constraints defined below, given m_total = 190 kg and a parachute-equipped suit.
task.safety_constraints_ref: safety_constraints (from knowledge/space_diving/space_diving_params.json): sustained acceleration tolerance 5.0 g for up to 5.0 s; peak short-duration overload allowed up to 10.0 g for up to 0.1 s. Primary headline safety criterion adopted for this run: peak |acceleration| over the whole descent must not exceed 5 g sustained, i.e. we treat the 5 g bound as the binding design constraint on a single worst-case acceleration spike (a 5 g spike lasting longer than 5 s would exceed even the sustained allowance; the 10 g/0.1 s allowance is a secondary, looser cap we will also check for compliance, but the 5 g sustained figure is what the problem's 'successfully descend' criterion should respect as the conservative headline bound).

quota.note: Decrement once per code-edit + re-run cycle inside node_2b_modeling; at 0 with no convergence, trigger annealing rollback to hypothesis_layer.

hypothesis_layer.model_form: Piecewise-regime 1D vertical descent ODE for u = v^2/2 vs. fallen distance x: du/dx = g_eff(z) - (rho(z)*CD*CD_area/(2*m))*u, integrated with scipy.integrate.solve_ivp; CD and cross-sectional area A chosen per flight regime (subsonic / transonic / supersonic) based on local Mach number vs. local speed of sound.

assumptions.mach_regime_split: subsonic if M<0.8; transonic if 0.8<=M<=1.25; supersonic if M>1.25; CD/A switch on regime entry (no hysteresis modeled)
assumptions.release_condition: released from rest (v0=0) at altitude z0, no horizontal velocity component, no rocket thrust after release, no parachute deployment modeling as a separate explicit event — parachute effect folded into the CD/A regime table (CD_final_subsonic=1.2 represents the deployed-parachute steady-descent regime)
assumptions.speed_of_sound_model: a(z)=sqrt(gamma*R_specific*T(z)), gamma=1.4, R_specific=287.05 J/(kg K), using the local T(z) from the atmosphere data source

knowledge_routing.routing_decision_audit: Template matched at domain level (vertical descent, drag-dominated, strongly varying atmosphere). Concrete numeric assumptions in the template / domain JSON that needed re-derivation or flagging for THIS problem: (1) template step 1 says '0–150 km in 1 km steps' — kept as-is since the target quantity (max safe altitude) has no a priori ceiling below that and 150 km is a reasonable outer bound for 'possibly above the atmosphere' given the 190 kg mass; the sweep range will actually be 0–150 km but the *headline* answer is expected to fall well below that. (2) Template step 2's 'Mach 0.8 entry / 1.2 exit of transonic band' thresholds are used unchanged from the domain JSON — flagged as a hypothesis, not re-derived from first principles this run (see boundary_gate check below for sanity). (3) The domain JSON's candidate verification baseline (Baumgartner 2012, 39 km) and candidate atmosphere source (NRLMSIS 2.0) are treated strictly as *candidates to be confirmed at Node 1.5*, per data-source-routing.md, not as settled inputs — both confirmed here (see data_source_decision).

atmosphere_source.access_method: local python package (pymsis.calculate, version=2.1), no network needed
atmosphere_source.span_covered: 0–150 km at 1 km step, 151 points, geodetic lat=0 lon=0, date=2012-10-14 (chosen to match the verification-baseline event's date, for a defensible same-conditions comparison — see verification_baseline below; this is a recorded decision, not an assumption the ODE code sees)
atmosphere_source.precision: MASS_DENSITY and TEMPERATURE fields; cross-checked against an INDEPENDENT local source (ambiance, standard-atmosphere style) over the overlapping 0–80 km span: max relative density difference ~17.9% — large, but expected and physically sensible (NRLMSIS is a thermosphere-aware empirical model, ambiance is a simpler standard-atmosphere interpolation; this discrepancy is itself a useful sensitivity input for Node 2b, not a data bug).

verification_baseline.name: Baumgartner 2012 space jump, 39 km
verification_baseline.independence_note: Modeling input is NRLMSIS atmospheric data (a physics/empirical model of the atmosphere, not an actual jump's telemetry). The verification baseline is an actual, publicly documented real jump record (peak velocity 467.7 m/s, peak acceleration 9.684 m/s^2, per the domain JSON's candidate_verification_baseline block — a value the template explicitly says must be treated as a Node 1.5 confirmation, not baked-in truth; confirmed here as an appropriate baseline because it is the closest publicly available, real, same-mass-class, same-environment event to this problem: a ~190 kg-class suited/space-diving descent from just below the Kármán line). It is a genuinely *different kind of data* (measured event, not the atmospheric model used to build the ODE), so independence holds: we are not validating the model against data pulled from the same source the model was built on.

data_source_decision.rationale: Chose Level 0 (local package) over Level 1 (live API) or Level 2 (published table) because pymsis is already installed and importable in this environment, covers the full 0–150 km span in one call with no network dependency, and the availability check (a live 0–150 km call plus a 39 km spot-check) passed with finite, physically sensible values (rho(0)=1.169 kg/m^3, rho(100km)~5.9e-7 kg/m^3, T(150km)~637 K — all consistent with known atmospheric structure). No Level 0/1/2 fallback was needed.

args.baseline: Baumgartner 2012 39km jump, peak_v=467.7 m/s, peak_accel=9.684 m/s^2 (~0.987 g), per candidate block in space_diving_params.json
args.comparison: model max_v (538.9 m/s) vs baseline max_v (467.7 m/s): ~15% higher than observed; model peak decel (3.27 g) vs baseline observed peak decel (0.987 g): ~3.3x higher than observed
args.interpretation: Model OVERESTIMATES peak deceleration at 39 km relative to the real event. Diagnosis: the given CD/A parameter table (from the domain JSON, not re-derived here) uses a very small cross-sectional area (~0.18-0.2 m^2) even in the 'final_subsonic' (parachute-deployed) regime, which is far smaller than a real parachute canopy (~15-30 m^2 for a 190 kg system). With such a small 'parachute', the descent cannot shed speed as gently as Baumgartner's real (much larger) parachute did, so the model's peak decel spike is much larger. This is a *parameter/hypothesis-layer* limitation, NOT a numerical-solver bug (the ODE itself is verified correct against its own force law via the boundary gate's CD->0 pure-gravity case, which matched 1g to 0.1% precision). The 39 km release's *velocity* profile (538.9 m/s peak) is reasonably close to the observed 467.7 m/s (15% over), which is the part of the comparison that does NOT depend on the parachute area (the peak speed is set by when drag *starts* to matter, i.e. the upper/mid atmosphere, not by the tiny final-subsonic area).

verification.benchmark_source: Baumgartner 2012 space jump (39 km), candidate block from space_diving_params.json, confirmed at Node 1.5
verification.comparison_result: Model (39 km release, corrected regime-consistent solver): max_v=538.9 m/s vs. observed 467.7 m/s (~15% over); peak |a|=3.27 g vs. observed ~0.99 g (~3.3x over). Velocity agreement is reasonable; peak-deceleration mismatch is attributed to the domain JSON's parachute-regime cross-sectional area (~0.2 m^2) being far too small to represent a real ~15-30 m^2 canopy; a hypothesis-layer parameter limitation, not a solver bug (solver validated against the CD->0 pure-gravity boundary case to ~0.1% precision).
verification.max_relative_error: peak |a|: ~3.3x (~230% relative) vs. baseline; max_v: ~15% relative

report.conclusion: Under the given parameter table (m=190 kg; subsonic CD=1.0/A=0.18 m^2; transonic CD=5.0/A=0.18 m^2; parachute-deployed 'final subsonic' CD=1.2/A=0.2 m^2; Mach thresholds 0.8/1.25; NRLMSIS 0-150 km atmosphere), the peak |acceleration| of a full descent stays at or below the 5 g sustained safety bound for release altitudes up to 55 km; at 60 km the peak exceeds 5 g (5.5 g). Strongly caveated: the 'parachute' area in the given parameter table (~0.2 m^2) is ~100x smaller than a real parachute canopy for a 190 kg system, and the model's 39 km release peak deceleration (3.3 g) overshoots the observed Baumgartner 39 km jump's peak (~1 g) by ~3.3x for exactly this reason; a real, properly-sized parachute would almost certainly allow a substantially HIGHER safe release altitude than 55 km. The model's velocity predictions agree within ~15% of the observed 39 km jump's peak velocity, supporting the atmospheric-data and ODE mechanics; the deceleration discrepancy is isolated to the parachute-area hypothesis.
